intro.html: Manners are the small ways we show other people that they matter: a greeting, a careful word, a secret kept. This topic’s words describe people by their manners, from the gracious to the gruff. Notice how many of the rude words are about how something is said (too short, too rough, too mean) rather than how loud it is.

Polite: courteous (respectful), tactful (spares feelings), discreet (keeps things private), urbane (polished and at ease), suave (smoothly charming). Rude: boorish (rough and loud), brusque (abrupt), curt (rudely brief), uncouth (without manners), churlish (mean and ungracious).

words.ex: The {courteous} bus driver waited for the running boy and greeted him with a smile.
words.ctx: Even when the customer began to shout, the clerk stayed {courteous}, thanking him for his patience and calmly offering to fix the order.
words.etym: From Old French corteis, “having manners fit for a royal court.”

mn.cue: manners fit for a royal COURT
mn.text: Sami bows to the queen and says, “Good morning, Your Majesty.” Manners fit for a royal court are {courteous}.

scene.alt: A boy bows politely to a smiling queen in her throne room.

words.def: careful to say things without hurting anyone’s feelings
words.ex: Felix gave a {tactful} answer when his aunt asked whether he liked her very orange sweater.
words.ctx: Rather than calling the essay boring, the teacher was {tactful}: she praised its strong opening and suggested ways to make the middle livelier.
words.etym: From tact, which comes from Latin tactus, “touch.”

mn.text: Tact comes from the Latin for touch. Aunt Greta asks if Felix likes her bright orange sweater, and he answers with a light touch: “It’s so cheerful!” He is {tactful}.

scene.alt: A woman in a loud orange dress asks her nephew if he likes it, and he answers kindly.

words.def: careful in what one says or does, especially in keeping secrets
words.ex: Be {discreet} about the surprise party; Grandma notices everything.
words.ctx: The nurse was always {discreet}: she never mentioned a patient’s name outside the clinic, not even at home with her own family.
words.etym: From Latin discretus, “separated,” from discernere, “to tell apart”: a discreet person can tell what to say from what to keep.
words.note: Discreet (careful, private) is not discrete (separate, distinct). Both come from the same Latin word but have gone separate ways.

mn.text: Zoe whispers her news, and Kai zips his lips: “This secret stays with me.” He never tells a soul. Kai is {discreet}.

scene.alt: A girl whispers a secret to a boy, who puts a finger to his lips; a padlock floats beside him.

words.def: polished, courteous and at ease in any social setting
words.ex: The {urbane} host remembered every guest’s name and made each one feel welcome.
words.ctx: Though he had grown up on a remote ranch, Marcus became an {urbane} diplomat, as comfortable at a formal dinner as at a cattle auction.
words.etym: From Latin urbanus, “of the city,” from urbs, city; city manners were thought to be polished.
words.note: Urban (of the city) and urbane (polished in manner) share the Latin urbs, city, but urbane is about manners, not places.

mn.text: At the museum gala, Victor greets each guest by name, bows, and tells just the right joke. His manners are city-polished: he is {urbane}.

scene.alt: A gentleman in a top hat bows gracefully to welcome a guest at a museum party.

words.def: charming, confident and smooth in manner
words.ex: The {suave} magician bowed, winked and pulled a rose from behind his hat.
words.ctx: Her brother tried to look {suave} at the dance, but the effect was spoiled when he tripped over his own feet and spilled punch down his shirt.
words.note: Suave is often praise, but it can hint that the charm is a little too smooth to trust.

mn.text: Spell it out: Smooth, Unruffled, At ease, Very charming, Elegant. Jamal glides across the stage in his bow tie and never misses a step: he is {suave}.

scene.alt: A man in a bow tie and sunglasses dances smoothly in a spotlight on stage.

words.ex: His {boorish} habit of talking with his mouth full annoyed everyone at the table.
words.ctx: The other guests were chatting quietly, so his {boorish} behavior stood out: he shouted across the room, put his feet on a chair and grabbed the last rolls.

mn.cue: a BOAR at the dinner table
mn.text: Picture a wild boar at a dinner party: snorting, grabbing, crumbs everywhere. Rex eats just like one. He is {boorish}.

labels.text: BOOR = a BOAR at the table

scene.alt: A rude man gobbles pizza and shouts for more beside a piggy; an old woman looks disgusted.

words.def: abrupt and short in speech or manner
words.ex: The busy clerk gave a {brusque} nod and turned to the next customer.
words.ctx: Usually warm and chatty, the coach was {brusque} that morning: he said “Laps. Now.” and walked off before anyone could ask a question.
words.etym: From French brusque, “lively, fierce,” from Italian brusco, “sour.”

mn.text: Nell asks a hurrying man for directions, and he brushes her off with one word, “Busy,” and keeps walking. A brush-off that quick is {brusque}.

scene.alt: At a train station, a hurrying man brushes off a woman asking for directions.

words.ctx: I wrote a long, friendly letter asking for help, but the reply was {curt}: just two words, “Not possible,” and not even a signature.

mn.text: Zoe starts to show the banker her whole plan for a lemonade stand, and he cuts her short: “No.” A reply cut that short is {curt}.

scene.alt: A girl holds up her plan to show a banker, who crosses his arms and says only no.

words.ex: Talking loudly on the phone all through the movie was {uncouth}.
words.ctx: In the old story, the {uncouth} giant wiped his hands on the tablecloth and stomped across the clean floor in muddy boots, to the queen’s horror.
words.etym: From Old English uncuth, “unknown, strange”: un (not) + cuth (known).

mn.text: It rhymes: the youth with no manners is uncouth. Jonah stomps into the quiet library in muddy boots, yelling for his friend. He is {uncouth}.

scene.alt: A muddy teenager shouts in a quiet library while a reader glares at him.

words.ex: It would be {churlish} to refuse a gift from a friend who saved for months to buy it.
words.ctx: After the neighbors spent all day fixing his fence, it was {churlish} of him to complain that they had painted it the wrong shade of white.

mn.text: Ivy gives Uncle Marcus a scarf she knitted herself, and he hurls it back with a grunt: “Itchy.” Hurling back a kind gift is {churlish}.

scene.alt: A grumpy man tosses back a gift from a girl, who is sad.

head: word
what is wrong (or right) with the manner
rows: abrupt: few words, no warmth, a hurry to be done
rudely brief: the shortness itself is the insult
rough and loud: no care for anyone around
unpolished: never learned the manners at all
mean and ungracious: answering kindness with rudeness
polished and at ease: the opposite of uncouth
after.cap: The rude words are not interchangeable: each one names a different fault.

after.html: discreet (careful, good at keeping secrets) and discrete (separate: “three discrete steps”) sound the same. Remember: a discreet friend keeps the secret; in discrete the t separates the two e’s.

items.q: Mom hid the birthday presents and told no one where. She was…
items.why: Discreet means careful about keeping private things private. Discrete means separate.

items.q: True or false: a brusque answer has to be shouted.
items.why: False. Brusque and curt describe answers that are abrupt and too short, not loud. A brusque “Fine” can be spoken quietly.

choices: The urbane ambassador put every nervous guest at ease.
We moved from the farm to an urbane apartment downtown.
The urbane traffic made us late.
items.why: Urbane describes polished, easy manners. For things that are simply in a city, the word is urban.

items.q: Kai’s friends threw him a surprise party, and he complained that the cake was the wrong flavor. His complaint was…
items.why: Answering kindness with rude, ungrateful complaints is churlish.

items.q: Type the word: careful to say things without hurting feelings (it comes from the Latin for touch).
items.why: Tactful: tact comes from Latin tactus, touch. A tactful person handles feelings with a light touch.
